records.title: 1.4 Turbo (A14NET) Timing Chain Stretch
records.description: The A14NET 1.4 turbo engine in Astra J/K, Corsa D/E, Mokka A, and Adam can suffer timing chain stretch typically between 80,000-140,000 km. IMPORTANT DIAGNOSTIC DISTINCTION: brief (1-3 second) rattle ONLY on cold start is more often a worn dual-mass flywheel — see Vauxhall TSB E-14-3157 for 2010-2014 A14NET. Persistent rattle, misfire codes, or rattle that extends beyond cold start point to timing chain stretch. Chain skip causes valve-piston contact.
records.solution: Diagnose before replacing — TSB E-14-3157 DMF replacement (€700-€1,200) for startup-only rattle. Full timing chain kit (chain, tensioner, guides, sprockets) €900-€1,500 for persistent rattle / misfire codes. Catastrophic failure means engine rebuild (€4,000+). Use full-synthetic 5W-30 (dexos2) and stick to 10,000 km intervals.

records.title: Astra H Ignition Barrel / Steering Column Lock Jamming (Key Won't Turn)
records.description: A widespread Astra H (2004-2010) failure documented across UK and German owner communities: the ignition barrel and mechanical steering column lock jam, so the key cannot be turned and the car will not start. Two failure modes are documented: a small pin on the back of the lock barrel wears a channel into its housing and jams, and a spring-loaded plastic plunger (the key-in-ignition detector) sticks due to accumulated grime, so the lock no longer registers the key. The steering lock can also bind against steering pre-load — many breakdown call-outs are resolved simply by rocking the steering wheel while turning the key. On pre-2008 cars, the related CIM (Column Integration Module) had software/hardware faults causing no-start and steering lock errors, which Opel addressed with updated software from model year 2008.
records.solution: If stranded, firmly rock the steering wheel left-right while gently turning the key to unload the lock bolt — this resolves many cases. Penetrating oil or electrical contact cleaner into the barrel can temporarily free a sticking plunger, but the fault typically returns; the lasting fix is replacing the ignition lock barrel (an auto locksmith can often code it to the existing key, which is cheaper than a dealer barrel + new keys). If the fault is electronic (no-start with steering lock error messages, pre-2008 cars), have the CIM software updated or the CIM replaced and coded by a dealer or specialist.
symptoms: Key will not turn in the ignition
Intermittent no-start that improves after wiggling the steering wheel
Key turns but car does not recognize it
Radio stays on after key removal

records.title: Astra J Electronic Parking Brake Faults and Hill-Start Assist Rollback Recall (15-R-058)
records.description: Two related problems affect the Astra J's electronic parking brake (EPB). First, an official recall: in July 2015 Opel recalled 136,830 Astra J, Cascada and Zafira Tourer vehicles in Germany (model years 2010-2015, manual transmission with EPB and hill-start assist) under campaign 15-R-058 because a software error in the hill-start assist could create the false impression of an engaged parking brake, allowing the car to roll away on a slope. Second, owner forums (MOTOR-TALK, astra-j.de) document recurring EPB hardware faults outside the recall: a failing centre-console EPB switch (a known cheap culprit, ~EUR 20 part), seized rear caliper actuators/cables, and in worse cases a failed EPB control module that is labour-intensive to replace. Symptoms range from a 'parking brake fault' warning to the brake refusing to apply or release, immobilising the car.
records.solution: First, check with an Opel dealer whether recall 15-R-058 (hill-start assist software update, ~30 minutes of work, free of charge) was performed on the vehicle. For EPB faults: read fault codes before replacing parts. Test the console switch first (inexpensive and a frequent cause); if voltage reaches the switch and bridging the connector actuates the motors, replace the switch. Otherwise inspect rear caliper actuators and cables for seizure — seized rear calipers typically need replacement in pairs. A defective EPB control module is the most expensive outcome. Always park in gear on slopes until the system is repaired.

Car rolls back on a hill despite hill-start assist
Grinding or squeaking from rear brakes

records.title: Astra K 1.6 CDTI "Whisper Diesel" EGR Cooler Internal Leak and DPF Clogging
records.description: The 1.6 CDTI (B16DTH/B16DTE) "Whisper Diesel" in the Astra K suffers from a well-documented EGR cooler failure: the cooler's internal sleeve cracks, letting coolant leak into the intake/exhaust tract. Owners report white smoke at start-up, unexplained coolant loss with no visible external leak, and exhaust smell inside the cabin. UK owners on Astra K Forums report a cluster of EGR and DPF failures, several after the diesel emissions software update, with code P0401 (insufficient EGR flow) commonly logged. The same engine is also prone to DPF clogging on short-trip use and to injection-quantity drift on individual injectors, compounding rough running. German forums (astra-k-forum.de) and German troubleshooting sites document identical failures, making this a cross-market consensus issue for 2015-2019 diesel Astra K models.
records.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the EGR cooler for internal leakage; check for coolant residue in the intake tract. Vauxhall/Opel sells the complete EGR cooler/valve assembly (around GBP 800-1000 in parts), but the cracked cooler sleeve alone is available as a separate part for roughly GBP 80 plus about an hour of labour, so insist on a sleeve-level repair quote first. Clean or force-regenerate the DPF if short-trip clogging is present, and have injector quantity corrections read out; replace and code any injector outside tolerance. Avoid sustained short-trip driving with this engine.
symptoms: White smoke from exhaust at cold start
Coolant level drops with no visible leak
Check engine light with code P0401
Frequent DPF regenerations or DPF warning
Rough running or jerking at light load

records.title: Astra K 1.6 Diesel Brake Fluid Contamination Recall — Reduced Braking Performance (18-C-120)
records.description: Official safety recall affecting Astra K 1.6-litre diesel models with manual transmission built from 23 March 2015 to 15 August 2018 (over 37,000 vehicles in the UK alone, plus German-market cars; campaign 18-C-120). On any used Astra K 1.6 diesel manual from this build window, confirm recall completion before purchase. If the brake pedal feels long or braking effort has increased on an unrepaired car, stop driving it and have the hydraulic system inspected immediately.

records.title: Astra L 1.2 Turbo (PureTech) Wet Timing Belt Premature Degradation
records.description: The Astra L's 1.2 Direct Injection Turbo three-cylinder (PSA/Stellantis PureTech EB2 family) uses a timing belt that runs inside the engine oil ("wet belt"). German automotive press (AUTO BILD, auto motor und sport) and Astra owner forums document the belt swelling, cracking and shedding material long before the official 100,000 km / 6-year interval. Shed belt particles clog the oil pick-up strainer, collapsing oil pressure; in the worst case the belt fails entirely and pistons hit valves, destroying the engine. Oil condition is the trigger: fuel dilution from short trips, aged oil, wrong oil spec or stretched service intervals chemically attack the belt. Stellantis responded with a reinforced belt in production from 2022, goodwill coverage of belt-related damage up to 175,000 km / 10 years under conditions (documented service history), and a switch to a timing chain on the third-generation 1.2 from 2023 — so Astra L buyers should verify per build date which timing drive their engine has.
records.solution: Verify the engine version by build date: early Astra L 1.2 Turbos (2022 into 2023 production) have the wet belt; the Gen-3 1.2 (from late 2023, including the new hybrid) uses a chain and is not affected. For wet-belt cars: use only oil meeting the exact Stellantis specification (PSA B71 2010 / 0W-20 as specified), change it strictly on or before schedule, and avoid chronic short-trip use. Have the belt inspected via the oil filler/inspection method (a low-cost belt-wear gauge exists) and replace it early at any sign of swelling or fraying, including cleaning the oil pick-up strainer. If damage occurred within 175,000 km / 10 years with full service history, claim goodwill coverage from Opel/Stellantis before paying out of pocket.
symptoms: Rattling or whining from the timing cover area
Black rubber debris in the oil or oil filler neck
Loss of power or engine failure

records.title: Astra H Rear Axle Bush Wear + Suspension Mount Corrosion (Salt-Belt)
records.description: Astra H rear suspension fails MOT in two common ways: (1) rear axle bushes / trailing-arm-pivot bushes show excessive movement, and (2) suspension mount areas in the bodyshell corrode in salt-belt markets (UK, Germany, Scandinavia, US Northeast). Both typically present at 8+ years old. Bushes alone are a moderate repair; mount corrosion can be a write-off if the chassis section is rotted.
records.solution: Rear axle bush replacement: 3-4 hours labor, £175-£280 / €200-€350. Suspension mount corrosion repair: depends on extent — minor patch welds €200-€500, structural sections €600-€1,500. Inspect annually after age 8 in salt regions; underseal proactively at year 5.

records.title: Astra H Water Pump Failure (Z16XEP Twinport / Z18XER 1.8)
records.description: Astra H (2004-2010) water pump failure is common between 60,000-130,000 km. The Z16XEP 1.6 Twinport drives its water pump from the AUX belt — leaks show first as coolant under the pulley side. The Z18XER 1.8 drives the pump from the timing belt — that pump must be replaced WITH the cambelt service. Both share plastic-impeller failure modes and often co-fail with the thermostat housing.
records.solution: Z16XEP: water pump replacement is a stand-alone job (€150-€300 incl. labor) once aux belt is off. Z18XER: do water pump AT the timing-belt service interval (~€400-€700 combined). Replace thermostat housing at the same time — same plastic-degradation issue.

records.title: Astra J 1.7 CDTI EGR Valve Clogging
records.description: The A17DTR/A17DTS 1.7 CDTI diesel in Astra J (2009-2015), Mokka A, and Meriva B suffers severe EGR valve carbon buildup, typically presenting between 80,000-150,000 km. Symptoms include power loss, limp mode, and rough idle. The EGR cooler can also crack, mixing coolant with intake flow.
records.solution: EGR valve clean or replacement (€400-€800 incl. labor). EGR delete is common but illegal in most markets and fails TÜV / MOT emissions tests. Walnut blasting helps the intake manifold simultaneously.

records.title: 1.2 PureTech petrol wet timing belt premature failure (engine destruction risk)
records.description: The 1.2 PureTech (EB2 family) three-cylinder petrol engine used in the Opel Combo / Combo Life uses a 'wet' timing belt that runs submerged in engine oil. The belt material degrades prematurely when the oil deteriorates (extended service intervals, wrong oil spec, or fuel dilution of the oil). As it breaks down, the belt sheds rubber particles into the oil, which clog the oil pump pickup, oil pump strainer and VVT solenoids, causing oil starvation. In the worst case the belt strips or snaps, and because it is an interference engine, valves collide with pistons and the engine is destroyed. Stellantis has acknowledged the defect, reduced service/belt intervals, and extended warranty coverage (up to ~10 years / ~112,000 miles) plus a claims portal for repair-cost reimbursement.
records.solution: Service the engine annually with the exact correct low-SAPS oil specification and never exceed the (revised, shortened) oil-change and belt-replacement intervals. Have the wet timing belt and oil pump strainer inspected/replaced early per the updated Stellantis schedule. If the car qualifies, claim repair costs through the Stellantis PureTech goodwill/warranty portal. Some specialists convert affected engines to an upgraded belt or recommend earlier renewal; a failed belt usually means a replacement or rebuilt engine.
symptoms: Rattling or whirring noise from the timing belt area
Rubber debris/sludge in the oil filter or oil
Oil warning light / low oil pressure
High oil consumption (up to ~1L per 1000 miles)
Loss of power or rough running
Engine fails to start or seizes after belt failure

records.title: 1.5 BlueHDi (DV5R) diesel fuel rail leak with engine-bay fire risk
records.description: On Combo diesels fitted with the 1.5 BlueHDi DV5R engine, the common-rail fuel distributor (high-pressure rail) cone may fail to maintain its circular shape, allowing the retaining nut to loosen. This was recalled across 14 Stellantis models including the Opel Combo built July to October 2025. A related newer DV5 recall also covers a NOx sensor that may not be properly tightened.
records.solution: Take the vehicle to an authorised dealer for the recall. Technicians inspect/replace the high-pressure fuel rail and ensure the rail cone/nut interface is correctly formed and torqued so fuel cannot escape. Owners of recent diesel Combos should check their VIN against the recall database and act on any leak smell of diesel immediately.

records.title: Diesel AdBlue / SCR system failure preventing engine restart
records.description: Combo diesels with the BlueHDi SCR (AdBlue) emissions system can display escalating warnings such as 'Add AdBlue: Start impossible in X km' or 'Engine restart disabled in X km'. Beyond simply running low on AdBlue, the warnings are commonly triggered by SCR/NOx sensor faults, AdBlue tank-level or quality sensor errors, AdBlue crystallisation, or the use of non-ISO 22241 fluid. Once the countdown reaches zero the ECU disables engine restart by emissions regulation, leaving the owner stranded.
records.solution: Top up with genuine ISO 22241-compliant AdBlue and complete a steady driving cycle to let the ECU validate the correction. If the warning persists, have the SCR system, NOx sensors and AdBlue level/quality sensors diagnosed (Opel MDI/diagnostic tool) and replace the faulty sensor or injector. Avoid cheap/contaminated AdBlue, which damages the SCR catalyst and sensors. Crystallised AdBlue lines may need cleaning/replacement.
symptoms: Engine will not restart once countdown expires

records.title: Diesel EGR valve and DPF clogging on short-journey use
records.description: Combo diesels (1.5 BlueHDi) used mainly for short, low-speed urban trips suffer from EGR valve carbon build-up and diesel particulate filter (DPF) blockage. The engine never reaches the temperature needed for passive/active DPF regeneration, so soot accumulates. A clogged DPF raises exhaust back-pressure, which alters EGR flow, while a sooty EGR increases soot output, creating a feedback loop that produces multiple emissions faults at once. Symptoms include rough idle, power loss, higher fuel use and limp mode. This is a well-known characteristic of the PSA/Stellantis diesels shared with the Berlingo/Rifter.
records.solution: Drive for at least 10-15 minutes at 65 km/h (~40 mph) or more regularly to allow the DPF to regenerate. Use the correct low-ash (low-SAPS) diesel oil. If already clogged, perform a forced regeneration via diagnostics, clean or replace the EGR valve, and clean or replace the DPF. Address any leaking injectors or weak turbo boost that overload the DPF with soot. Buyers doing only short trips should consider the petrol model instead of the diesel.

records.title: Corsa D Front Subframe (Axle Carrier) Corrosion
records.description: The Corsa D's front subframe (Achskörper/Fahrschemel — the axle carrier the lower control arms and steering rack bolt to) is a known rust weak point. If corrosion is advanced or perforated, replace the axle carrier (new parts roughly €140-600; powder-coated replacements are recommended) — all stretch/tension bolts must be renewed and a wheel alignment performed afterwards. A professional replacement including alignment typically runs around €800.

records.title: Corsa D Heater Blower Resistor Failure — Fan Only Works on Speed 4
records.description: An extremely common Corsa D fault: the heater blower works only on the highest setting (speed 4) while speeds 1-3 are dead. Speed 4 feeds the blower motor directly, so it keeps working when the resistor pack that drops voltage for the lower speeds fails — usually because its integrated thermal fuse blows. The resistor pack sits behind the heater body and its wiring connector frequently overheats and melts, sometimes damaging the loom and requiring a repair connector. A worn, stiff blower motor drawing excess current is often the underlying reason the thermal fuse blows, so resistor failures can recur. Documented across UK and German owner forums with dedicated repair videos; OE part numbers 55702407 / 13248240.
records.solution: Replace the heater blower resistor pack (GM part 55702407 / 13248240, roughly £15-35) — it is accessible behind the glovebox/heater body and is a common DIY job. Inspect the wiring connector for heat damage and fit a repair pigtail if melted. If the resistor fails again quickly, replace or lubricate the blower motor, as a worn motor drawing high current is what blows the resistor's thermal fuse.
symptoms: Heater fan only works on speed 4 (full)
Intermittent blower operation before total failure of lower speeds
Melted or scorched resistor wiring connector

records.title: Corsa-e On-Board Charger Fault — 'Electric Traction System Fault' / 'Battery Charge Fault'
records.description: Battery-electric Corsa-e (Corsa Electric) models on the Stellantis e-CMP platform suffer a recurring 'Electric traction system fault: Repair needed' and 'Battery charge fault: Stop the vehicle' warning, typically appearing during or right after charging. Affected cars can refuse to charge, lose drive power, or be unable to restart for several minutes. Stellantis traced part of the problem to a non-compliant on-board charger (OBC) and ran a recall/service campaign in EU markets under which dealers read out diagnostic trouble codes, update software and replace the OBC where necessary, free of charge. Owner forums (SpeakEV, Opel Corsa forums) document multiple cases, with fixes ranging from OBC replacement to battery charge monitoring module (BECB) replacement; a weak 12V auxiliary battery produces similar phantom faults.
records.solution: Have an Opel/Vauxhall dealer check whether the OBC recall/service campaign is outstanding for the VIN and read out the stored DTCs — the campaign includes a software update and OBC replacement where codes confirm the fault (a 3-6 hour job, free under the campaign). If faults persist, the battery charge monitoring module (BECB) may need replacement under warranty. Test and replace the 12V auxiliary battery if weak, as low 12V voltage triggers the same warnings; disconnecting the 12V battery for a few minutes clears the fault only temporarily.

records.title: Corsa F 1.2 PureTech Wet Timing Belt Premature Degradation
records.description: The Corsa F's 1.2 PureTech (EB2) three-cylinder petrol engine uses a 'wet' timing belt that runs inside the engine oil. The belt degrades prematurely — well before the official 100,000 mile / 10-year interval — as oil contaminated with unburned fuel attacks the belt material. Disintegrating belt debris clogs the oil pick-up and strainer, causing oil pressure loss, oil starvation and in the worst cases catastrophic engine failure when the belt skips or snaps. The problem is so widespread across Stellantis brands (Peugeot, Citroën, Opel/Vauxhall, DS) that Stellantis opened an official compensation platform and extended coverage to 10 years / 180,000 km for affected EB2 engines. UK Corsa owners report belts breaking up on 2020 cars, and the engine is also known for excessive oil consumption. Later Corsa hybrid engines (EB2LTEDH2, from the 2024 facelift) switched to a timing chain.
records.solution: Have the wet belt inspected (a degraded belt shows swelling and shed teeth visible through the oil filler or during endoscope inspection) and replaced early — many specialists recommend every 4-6 years / 50,000-60,000 miles instead of the factory interval. Use only oil meeting the PSA B71 2312 / Stellantis specification and shorten oil change intervals to roughly 10,000 km or annually. If the oil pressure light has come on, the sump and oil pick-up strainer must also be cleaned of belt debris. Check eligibility under the Stellantis 10-year/180,000 km extended warranty and compensation scheme for belt-related repairs performed between January 2022 and December 2024.
symptoms: Oil pressure warning light, especially after motorway driving
Rattling or rough running on cold start
Engine management light with reduced power (limp mode)
Black rubber belt debris visible under the oil filler cap or in the sump

records.title: Corsa D Handbrake — Lever Mechanism (CSP) + Cable Wear
records.description: Corsa D (2006-2014) has two related handbrake issues. (1) Lever-mechanism design: the release button could partially disengage the parking brake if the lever was applied incorrectly — Vauxhall ran a customer satisfaction programme offering a free modification. (2) Cable wear and binding: rear cables run under the car and suffer corrosion/seizing in salt regions, eventually failing MOT or refusing to release. Common at 6-10 years old.
records.solution: Check Vauxhall service-history records for the CSP modification — if not done, your dealer should still apply it free. Cable replacement €120-€280 incl. labor. Always test parking-brake hold on an incline periodically — failure can be sudden and silent.

records.title: Corsa D 1.2 / 1.4 Petrol Timing Chain Stretch
records.description: Naturally-aspirated 1.2 (Z12XEP/A12XER) and 1.4 (Z14XEP/A14XER) engines in Corsa D (and Adam) suffer timing chain stretch — distinct from the A14NET turbo issue. The 1.4 87hp shows first symptoms as early as 60,000-80,000 km; the 1.2 typically at 80,000-100,000 km. Root cause is tensioner bleed-off overnight + chain wear, worsened by long oil intervals or low-grade oil. Cold-start rattle (1-30 seconds) is the classic early sign.
records.solution: Chain kit replacement (chain, tensioner, guides) typically €700-€1,200. Some independents will polish the existing sprockets; OEM kit is the durable fix. Use the correct Dexos2 oil (5W-30) and stick to 10,000 km intervals at most.

records.title: Corsa E Electric Power Steering Column Failure
records.description: Corsa E (2014-2019) EPS column motor / control unit can fail, causing sudden loss of power assistance. Some Vauxhall warranty replacements have been recorded but no formal market-wide warranty-extension programme. The pattern is well-documented on Corsa C and D and continues on E. Sudden assistance loss while moving is possible.
records.solution: Replacement steering column assembly is the standard fix (€600-€1,200 dealer; refurbishment specialists offer rebuild at €300-€500). Always check service-history records for any goodwill replacements at the dealer; some owners have had part-funded repairs as a goodwill gesture even outside formal warranty.

records.title: Crossland 1.2 PureTech "Wet" Timing Belt Disintegration
records.description: The PSA EB2DTS 1.2 PureTech 3-cylinder turbo uses an oil-immersed ("wet") timing belt that degrades on standard mineral or low-quality synthetic oil. Belt particles clog the oil pickup strainer, starving the engine of oil and causing catastrophic damage. Affects post-2017 Crossland (and Citroën, Peugeot, DS variants of the same engine).
records.solution: Use ONLY Stellantis-approved Total Quartz INEO First 0W-30 (or equivalent C2 spec). Replace belt at 100,000 km / 6 years — earlier than original schedule (Stellantis revised guidance multiple times). Oil pickup strainer should be inspected if belt is overdue. Catastrophic failure means engine replacement (€5,000+).

records.title: 1.2 PureTech (EB2) Wet Timing Belt Degradation & Oil Starvation
records.description: Grandland X models with the 1.2 PureTech three-cylinder petrol engine (EB2/EB2ADTS, developed by PSA) use a 'wet' timing belt that runs submerged in engine oil. The belt coating breaks down over time, shedding rubber/material debris into the oil. This debris clogs the oil pump pickup strainer, VVT solenoids and oil passages, causing oil starvation and accelerated wear, and the belt can ultimately snap, causing catastrophic engine damage on this interference engine. Symptoms include rattling on cold start, oil/CEL warnings, ticking from the timing case and excessive oil consumption.
records.solution: Replace the wet timing belt well ahead of the original interval. Manufacturer guidance was revised down from ~180,000 km to roughly every 90,000-100,000 km (or 6 years); some specialists recommend even earlier inspection. Use only the correct low-SAPS oil and keep to short oil-change intervals to slow belt breakdown. If debris/oil starvation has occurred, the oil pump strainer, solenoids and possibly the engine must be inspected/replaced.
symptoms: Loss of power or sudden engine failure

records.title: Grandland X 1.6 THP Timing Chain Stretch
records.description: The PSA/BMW "Prince" 1.6 THP engine in early Grandland X (2017-2021) suffers timing chain stretch, also documented across Peugeot 3008/5008 and Citroën C5 Aircross. records.solution: Chain kit replacement €1,200-€2,000. Stick to 10,000 km oil intervals with full-synthetic C2/C3. Listen for the characteristic "death rattle" on cold start — once consistent, replacement is urgent.

records.title: Diesel SCR/AdBlue & NOx Sensor Emissions Fault with 'Starting Impossible' Limp Mode
records.description: Diesel Grandland X models (1.5 BlueHDi/1.6 diesel with SCR after-treatment) frequently throw exhaust after-treatment faults. Owners see emissions warnings, reduced power/limp mode, and the countdown message 'Engine start prevented in XXX miles/km'. Common root causes are NOx sensor failure (range/performance faults), SCR system or AdBlue injector/pump faults, crystallised AdBlue, or poor-quality urea. If ignored, the car eventually refuses to start. Critical phase is commonly around 30,000-45,000 km.
records.solution: Diagnose with a scan tool to identify whether the fault is a NOx sensor, the SCR/AdBlue dosing system, or sensor wiring/connector corrosion. Typical fixes: replace the failed NOx sensor (upstream/downstream), clean or replace the AdBlue injector/pump, refill with quality AdBlue, and clear the codes/reset the countdown. Software updates from Stellantis exist for some after-treatment faults. Do not ignore the 'start prevented' countdown.

records.title: EAT8 (Aisin AWF8) Automatic Transmission Jerking, Hesitation & Whining Noise
records.description: Grandland X models fitted with the Aisin EAT8 8-speed automatic (shared across the Stellantis/PSA platform with Peugeot/Citroen) exhibit poor low-speed shift quality once the gearbox is at operating temperature. Owners report gears 1-3 shifting very slowly with an extra throttle/RPM surge between shifts, jerking when pulling away from a stop, hesitation on kick-down, and harsh shifts when cold. A separate but common complaint is a loud metallic 'singing'/whining noise from the gearbox between roughly 45-65 km/h. Root cause is sensitivity of the EAT8 to learned adaptation values and (for the noise) gear/bearing tolerances dealers often dismiss as 'normal'.
records.solution: First step is a transmission adaptation reset followed by relearn drive cycle, plus any Opel/Stellantis transmission control software update; many cars improve significantly without mechanical repair. Persistent harsh shifting can require an ATF fluid level/quality check and service (the EAT8 needs the correct Aisin spec fluid). The whine is harder to resolve and sometimes requires valve body or gearbox replacement under warranty if severe.

records.title: Insignia A 2.0 CDTI EGR Cooler Crack (Coolant Loss into Intake)
records.description: The A20DT/A20DTH 2.0 CDTI EGR cooler develops internal cracks, allowing coolant to leak into the intake. Symptoms: white smoke from exhaust, mysterious coolant loss with no external leak, sweet smell, eventual no-start as cylinders flood. Common at 100,000-180,000 km. Same engine in Astra J, Zafira C, Cascada.
records.solution: EGR cooler replacement €600-€1,200 incl. labor. If coolant has been pulled into cylinders, hydrolock check required. Some independents recommend EGR delete + remap — illegal in most markets and disqualifies TÜV inspection.

records.title: Insignia A Aisin AF40 Harsh Shifts / Shudder
records.description: The Aisin AF40 6-speed automatic in Insignia A (2008-2017) develops harsh shifts, shudder during lock-up, and delayed engagement, typically by 100,000-160,000 km. Root cause is degraded ATF and worn solenoids; Opel's "lifetime fill" claim is widely disputed.
records.solution: Drain-and-fill ATF every 60,000 km using Aisin JWS3309 / Dexron VI-compatible fluid (~€150-€250 DIY). Solenoid pack replacement if shifts remain harsh (€500-€900). Full mechatronic / valve body rebuild €1,500-€2,500. Severe shudder may indicate torque converter wear.

records.title: Insignia A Flex-Pipe Exhaust Failure
records.description: Insignia A front exhaust flex section cracks/fractures around 80,000-150,000 km, especially on diesels. Produces loud rattling/blowing under acceleration, smell of fumes in cabin, and triggers a fault if the lambda sensor is downstream of the leak.
records.solution: Flex section can be cut out and replaced (independent specialist €120-€280) instead of buying the full front pipe. OEM full pipe €350-€600. Check downstream lambda sensor function after repair.

records.title: Insignia A 2.0 CDTI Premature Timing Belt / Water Pump Failure (Engine Destruction)
records.description: The 2.0 CDTI diesel (A20DTH/A20DTJ) in the Insignia A uses a timing belt on an interference engine, and German and UK owner communities document repeated belt failures well before the official 120,000-150,000 km / 10-year change interval. A common trigger is the belt-driven water pump seizing, which shreds or melts the belt — one documented UK case occurred at just 15,000 miles, another on a 2012 (62-plate) car. When the belt snaps, pistons strike the open valves, bending valves and snapping rocker arms, which typically destroys the cylinder head and often the whole engine. German maintenance guides explicitly warn of 'kapitaler Motorschaden' if the interval is stretched, and forum threads on Motor-Talk and Insignia-Freunde collect multiple total-loss engine failures.
records.solution: Replace the timing belt kit early and completely: belt, tensioner, idler rollers AND the water pump together, ideally every 90,000-100,000 km or 6 years rather than waiting for the maximum factory interval (German workshops quote roughly 450-750 EUR for the full job). Investigate any whining or grinding from the belt area or unexplained coolant loss immediately, since a failing water pump is the most common belt killer. If the belt has already snapped, the engine must be stripped: expect bent valves, damaged rockers and possible piston contact — repairs range from a cylinder head overhaul to a replacement engine.
symptoms: Sudden engine cut-out while driving with no restart
Engine cranks but will not start after the failure
Rattling or slapping noise from the timing cover area
Whining or grinding from a failing water pump
Unexplained coolant loss near the front of the engine

records.title: Insignia A 4x4 Haldex Coupling & Rear Differential Failure (Oil Mixing / Pump Failure)
records.description: Insignia A 4x4 models (including the OPC) suffer chronic failures of the rear drive unit: the shaft seal (Simmerring) between the rear differential and the Haldex coupling degrades, letting the two separate oil fills mix into sludge, while the Haldex hydraulic pump fails from contaminated, never-changed fluid. German forum consensus (Motor-Talk, Insignia-Freunde, opel-turbo.de) is that the root aggravator is Opel specifying NO regular Haldex oil change interval — unlike VW/Audi cars using the same Haldex hardware, which fail far less often. Symptoms are knocking, banging and juddering from the rear axle in tight low-speed turns, often initially without fault codes; failures are documented from under 43,000 km. A complete replacement rear axle drive unit costs around 4,000 EUR (differential alone ~2,000 EUR), and Opel historically covered up to 90% on goodwill for some owners.
records.solution: Preventive care is the cheap fix: change the Haldex oil (and clean the pump screen) every 40,000-60,000 km even though Opel does not require it, and have the diff to Haldex shaft seal checked for weeping whenever the car is on a lift. If knocking/juddering in tight corners has started, have the Haldex pump, fluid condition and seal inspected before the differential is damaged — a pump and oil service is a few hundred euros, while a worn-out unit means a ~2,000 EUR differential or ~4,000 EUR complete rear drive unit. After repair, the Haldex/ABS-ESP software may need reprogramming.

records.title: Insignia B 2.0 Diesel Fuel Line Chafing — Fire Risk (KBA Recall E191905110 / 20-C-012)
records.description: Official KBA-supervised recall: on Insignia B models with the 2.0-liter diesel built between July 2016 and November 2018, a faulty clamp/bracket can rub through the fuel line. Leaking diesel can reach hot engine components and cause an engine-bay fire. Roughly 45,000 vehicles were affected worldwide, 21,436 of them in Germany. The recall runs under KBA reference E191905110 (Opel campaign 20-C-012); German trade press (kfz-betrieb) and owner forums (Motor-Talk, 'Rückruf KBA 9541') document the campaign. The workshop remedy takes about 30 minutes: the clamp position and fuel line are inspected, the line is replaced if chafed, a spacer is exchanged and protective hose sleeving is added.
records.solution: Check whether the recall has been performed: enter the VIN on Opel's official recall-check page or ask any Opel dealer to query the campaign status (KBA E191905110 / Opel 20-C-012). If open, the dealer inspects the fuel line routing, replaces the damaged line where needed, fits a new spacer and adds protective sleeving — free of charge, about 30 minutes. Until the fix is done, investigate any diesel smell or visible wetness on fuel lines near the engine immediately and do not keep driving with an active fuel leak.

records.title: Insignia A Electric Parking Brake Actuator / Control Module Failure
records.description: The Insignia A uses a cable-pull electric parking brake whose central actuator motor and control electronics are a recurring failure point documented across German Opel forums since the car was new. Owners report the 'Check parking brake' / 'Fehler Parkbremse' warning appearing from as little as ~48,000 km, the EPB refusing to release (dragging rear wheels, car immobilized) or failing to clamp so the car rolls on a slope, and the dash switch going dead. The actuator motor (GM part 13582928) can run to full extension and jam if brake service is done without putting the system in service mode, and repeated repairs are documented — including cases where a replaced actuator failed again. Dealer replacement of the EPB control unit/actuator has been quoted at 1,500-2,000 EUR in forum reports; cheaper causes include a worn EPB switch or corroded/seized brake cables.
records.solution: Diagnose before replacing parts: read EPB fault codes and check the switch, cables and actuator individually — a corroded cable set or worn switch is far cheaper than the actuator/control unit. Always put the EPB into service mode (or use a diagnostic tester) before doing any rear brake work, otherwise the actuator can over-travel and jam. If the actuator motor or control module has failed, replacement (often with the latest software) is the fix; budget a few hundred euros for switch/cables up to 1,500-2,000 EUR for the dealer actuator/control-unit job. Freeing a stuck brake at the roadside may require manual release and a tow.

records.title: 1.2 PureTech Wet Timing Belt Degradation / Failure (Mokka B)
records.description: The second-generation Mokka B (built on the Stellantis CMP platform) uses the PSA/Stellantis 1.2 PureTech (EB2) three-cylinder turbo with a 'wet' timing belt that runs submerged in engine oil. Fuel dilution and oil contamination cause the belt rubber to break down prematurely; shed particles clog the oil pump pick-up strainer, starving the engine of oil, and the belt itself can skip teeth or snap. Because it is an interference engine, belt failure typically destroys valves and pistons. Affected cars also show excessive oil consumption. Stellantis acknowledged the defect and runs a PureTech compensation platform covering documented oil-consumption and premature-belt expenses on 1.0/1.2 PureTech cars, with extended warranty up to 10 years / 112,000 miles under conditions.
records.solution: Strictly follow the (shortened) oil-and-belt service interval with the correct low-SAPS oil; replace the wet belt, tensioner and oil pump strainer preventively (many indies convert/replace early). If oil consumption or belt debris is found, submit a claim through the Stellantis PureTech compensation portal / authorised dealer; catastrophic failures require a full engine rebuild or replacement.
symptoms: Loss of power or sudden engine failure

records.title: 1.4 Turbo Timing Chain Stretch / Cold-Start Rattle (A14NET/B14NET)
records.description: The 1.4 Turbo petrol (GM Family-0, A14NET/B14NET) fitted to the first-gen Mokka and Mokka X suffers from timing-chain stretch and tensioner/guide wear, often appearing from around 80,000-100,000 km. A stretched chain alters valve timing and, if it skips, can cause serious internal engine damage. The classic symptom is a metallic rattle for a few seconds on cold start. Owners on the Mokka Owners Club report needing chain, tensioner and sometimes turbo/water-pump work, with cars off the road for extended periods. Cars used mostly for short trips and frequent stop-start cycles tend to wear faster.
records.solution: Diagnose chain stretch via crank/cam correlation and cam-timing fault codes; replace the timing chain, tensioner, guides and sprockets as a kit, using genuine/quality parts and the correct oil and service intervals to prevent recurrence. Address any related turbo or water-pump wear at the same time while the front is apart.

records.title: 1.6 CDTI EGR Valve & Cooler Carbon Clogging (P0401)
records.description: The 1.6 CDTI diesel (B16DTH/B16DTU, 'Whisper Diesel') in the Mokka X is prone to heavy carbon build-up in the EGR valve, EGR cooler and intake, especially on city-driven cars. The ECU infers EGR flow from the MAF signal, so any restriction triggers P0401 (insufficient EGR flow) and rough running or limp mode. A separate failure is the vacuum-operated EGR-cooler bypass-flap actuator, whose spindle can snap. Forum reports (Mokka Owners Club) document recurring P0401, often combined with MAF/MAP faults.
records.solution: Remove and ultrasonically clean the EGR valve, throttle body and intake pipe; in many cases the EGR cooler is fully clogged or the bypass flap is broken and must be replaced. Verify MAF/MAP sensors and vacuum lines. Regular motorway runs and good-quality diesel reduce recurrence.

records.title: Mokka A 1.7 CDTI Water Pump / Timing Belt Drive
records.description: The 1.7 CDTI water pump is timing-belt-driven in this engine. When the pump seizes or its impeller fails, the timing belt can be ejected — leading to valve damage. Failure typically appears between 80,000-130,000 km, often before the recommended belt service.
records.solution: Replace water pump WITH timing belt as a kit (€700-€1,100) rather than belt alone. Catastrophic pump failure with belt jump means head rebuild (€2,500+). Do the kit early if there's any whining or weeping from the pump.

records.title: Air Conditioning Condenser Leak / Compressor Failure
records.description: The Mokka/Mokka X air-conditioning system frequently loses cooling performance at relatively low mileage. Common root causes are a leaking condenser (mounted low at the front and vulnerable to stone damage and corrosion), a defective expansion valve, or a failing compressor; 2018-build cars are noted as particularly affected. Owners report the system going empty repeatedly after being regassed, indicating an active refrigerant leak.
records.solution: Leak-test the system (UV dye / electronic sniffer / nitrogen pressure test) to locate the leak; replace the condenser, expansion valve or compressor as required, evacuate and recharge with the correct refrigerant and oil. Replacing the receiver/drier is recommended when the system is opened.

records.title: Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) Clogging & Failed Regeneration
records.description: On the CDTI diesel Mokka/Mokka X driven mainly on short city journeys, the DPF cannot reach the temperature needed for passive/active regeneration and progressively clogs with soot, often as early as 30,000-50,000 km. This produces reduced power, increased fuel use, repeated regeneration warnings and exhaust aftertreatment fault codes; a blocked DPF that never completes regeneration eventually needs forced regen or replacement. The issue is tightly linked to the EGR carbon problem on the same engines.
records.solution: Take the car on regular sustained motorway drives to allow active regeneration; when clogged, perform a forced (static) regeneration with a diagnostic tool or professional DPF clean. A failed/blocked filter must be replaced. Fix any underlying EGR, injector or sensor faults that prevent successful regen.

records.title: Dual-Mass Flywheel Rattle / Clutch Judder (Manual Diesel)
records.description: First-gen Mokka and Mokka X manual diesels (1.6/1.7 CDTI) commonly develop a metallic rattling or ringing noise from the bellhousing area, most noticeable at idle when warm or on the over-run. The cause is wear of the dual-mass flywheel's internal damper springs, sometimes accompanied by clutch judder on take-up. In advanced cases the pedal can stick and start-up becomes noisy. It is frequently misdiagnosed as an engine noise.
records.solution: Confirm DMF wear (excess rotational free-play, characteristic rattle) and replace the dual-mass flywheel; because the gearbox must come out, the clutch kit (and often the slave cylinder) is replaced at the same time to avoid duplicate labour.
symptoms: Metallic rattle/ringing from bellhousing at idle

records.title: Mokka-e 12V Auxiliary Battery Drain
records.description: Mokka-e (and closely related Corsa-e, Peugeot e-208, DS 3 Crossback E-Tense — all CMP/eCMP platform) drains the 12V AGM auxiliary battery during long parking spells, leaving the car unable to wake or charge. Owners report drain as fast as 3-5 days of inactivity. The MyOpel smartphone app polling the car wakes systems and accelerates drain. Stellantis acknowledged the issue and pushed multiple software updates between 2021-2024 — Opel recalled ~13,507 Corsa/Combo/Mokka in Germany alone for the traction battery control software.
records.solution: Update vehicle software to latest (dealer can check; some VINs covered by recall). Use a 12V battery maintainer for parked stretches over 1 week. Disable MyOpel remote polling if parking long-term. AGM 12V replacement needs coding — DIY is risky; dealer cost ~€290 (€150-€250 battery + €50-€100 fit/code).

records.title: Mokka-e Onboard AC Charger (Mahle 11kW) Failure
records.description: The electric Mokka-e (and Corsa-e platform sibling) suffers from failures of the Mahle 11 kW three-phase onboard charger (OBC). When it fails, the car can no longer AC charge from a home wallbox or public AC point (often showing 'charging at 0 miles per hour' or charging briefly then stopping); DC rapid charging may still work as a stop-gap. Forum reports indicate dealers replacing these units regularly, and out-of-warranty replacement is expensive (often over EUR 2,000). 2021-2022 cars are most cited. This is distinct from the separate 12V auxiliary-battery drain issue.
records.solution: Diagnose the OBC via dealer/EV specialist; the fix is replacement of the onboard charger module (covered under the EV-component / battery extended warranty where applicable). As a temporary workaround some owners reduce wallbox current (e.g. 32A to 16A) or use DC rapid charging until repaired.
symptoms: Cannot AC charge from wallbox/public charger
DC charging works but AC does not

records.title: Start-Stop System Malfunction / 12V Battery Parasitic Drain (ICE)
records.description: Combustion-engine Mokka/Mokka X owners frequently report the Start-Stop system ceasing to function alongside a flat or weak 12V battery, sometimes after the car stands for a week or two. The AGM/EFB battery and its state-of-charge management are central: when voltage dips below roughly 11.6V the ECU disables Start-Stop and can lose learned parameters. Some cases are simple battery wear or a marginal alternator, but persistent parasitic drains (modules not sleeping) have left some cars repeatedly going flat even after battery replacement.
records.solution: Test the battery and alternator first and fit the correct AGM/EFB battery with proper coding/registration; if drain persists, perform a parasitic-draw test to find the module/circuit staying awake and repair it. Ensure software is up to date.
symptoms: Repeated battery replacement without fixing drain

records.title: Vivaro B 1.6 BiTurbo CDTI (R9M) Timing Chain Stretch
records.description: The Renault-sourced R9M 1.6 BiTurbo CDTI used in Vivaro B (and Trafic III, Movano B) develops timing chain stretch, typically 100,000-180,000 km. Cold-start rattle, misfire codes, then potential chain skip causing valve damage. Particularly bad on stop-start fleet use without regular oil changes.
records.solution: Full chain kit (€1,200-€1,800) including chain, guides, tensioners, sprockets — full job often involves engine drop in vans due to tight clearance. Use C4-spec low-SAPS 5W-30 oil and shorten intervals to 15,000 km max for fleet/stop-start duty.

records.title: 1.6 CDTi Timing Chain Tensioner Failure and Chain Stretch (B16DTH/B16DTE/B16DTL)
records.description: The 'whisper diesel' 1.6 CDTi engines fitted to the Zafira Tourer C suffer a well-documented timing chain failure. The original chain tensioner lacks a gasket, so oil drains out of the tensioner when the engine is switched off. This produces a metallic rattle/ticking on cold start (typically 2-5 seconds) as the chain runs slack before oil pressure builds. Over time the chain stretches, the plastic guides wear, and in severe cases the chain can jump timing or snap, causing pistons to contact valves and destroying the engine. Failures are commonly reported well before 100,000 miles. The chain is at the rear of the engine (gearbox side), making it a labour-intensive repair.
records.solution: Replace the timing chain, both sprockets, guides and the uprated/gasketed tensioner as a kit (10-12 hours labour, often requiring engine/gearbox separation). Catch it early at the first cold-start rattle. Frequent oil changes with the correct dexos2 spec oil at 6,000-9,000 mile intervals slow chain wear. If the chain has already snapped, expect a full engine rebuild or replacement.
symptoms: Metallic rattle or ticking on cold start
Rattle from gearbox end of engine

records.title: 1.8 Petrol (Z18XER/A18XER) Coolant Leaks and Water Pump Failure
records.description: The 1.8 16V petrol engine (Z18XER, later A18XER) in the Zafira B is prone to coolant leaks. The water pump seal fails and weeps coolant from the pump pulley area (sometimes spraying onto the air-con compressor), and the plastic coolant pipes/housings and ageing hoses crack and seep. Owners also report the oil cooler/cooler seal weeping. If unnoticed the car loses coolant and can overheat. Note this engine is timing-BELT driven (not chain), so the belt and tensioner/water pump should be serviced together to avoid belt failure causing valve damage.
records.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system to pinpoint the leak. Replace the water pump (ideally with the timing belt and tensioner as a combined job, ~every 60k miles / belt interval), and renew cracked plastic coolant pipes, the thermostat housing and any perished hoses. Inspect the oil cooler seal. Use the correct long-life coolant.
symptoms: Coolant leak under car / low coolant level
Coolant spray around water pump pulley
Visible weeping from plastic coolant pipes

records.title: 1.9 CDTi Swirl Flap (Drallklappen) Linkage Failure (Z19DTH/Z19DT)
records.description: The 1.9 CDTi engines in the Zafira B use intake-manifold swirl flaps controlled by a plastic actuator linkage. The linkage rod and bushings wear or break, so the flaps no longer move correctly, triggering limp mode and stored fault codes P2279 (intake air system leak) and/or P2075 (intake manifold runner position sensor/switch). German owners (motor-talk.de, zafira-forum.de) report this commonly around 90,000-150,000 km, often alongside EGR and DPF clogging on the same engine. Left unrepaired, a flap can break off and be ingested by the engine.
records.solution: Fit a swirl flap linkage repair kit (replacement rod, bushings and clips) — a low-cost fix that restores flap movement; clear codes afterwards. Some owners delete/blank the swirl flaps where legal. Inspect and clean the EGR valve and intake at the same time, as carbon build-up worsens the problem.

records.title: Zafira B Fire Risk — HVAC Blower Resistor (2015-2016 Recall)
records.description: Official DVSA bulletin NCA/2015/026 covers right-hand-drive Vauxhall Zafira B model years 2005-2014 and states that an overheated heater-fan resistor can create a fire risk if the failed thermal fuse is manipulated or bypassed. Vauxhall then issued a second safety recall, 16-C-050, for Zafira B vehicles with manual air conditioning or without air conditioning, including vehicles already repaired under 15-C-097, because the resistor could degrade under specific circumstances and lead to fire.
records.solution: Check the VIN and heating/air-conditioning configuration with Vauxhall and complete every outstanding recall free of charge. The official second-recall repair uses a wax-fuse heater-fan resistor and water deflector and checks the blower motor for replacement. Until that repair, follow the current manufacturer instruction for the exact vehicle; the 2016 letter specifies fan setting 0 or 4 and setting 0 if speed 4 does not operate. Never bypass a thermal fuse. Do not buy or install a resistor, motor or wiring repair from this page; recall status and the authorized remedy are VIN-specific.

records.title: Zafira Tourer 1.6 CDTI EGR Cooler Failure
records.description: The B16DTH "Whisper Diesel" 1.6 CDTI in Zafira Tourer (and shared Astra J/K) suffers EGR cooler failure with similar symptoms to the 2.0 CDTI: coolant disappearing, white smoke, and sweet smell. Typical onset 80,000-150,000 km.
records.solution: EGR cooler assembly replacement €550-€1,100. Check for coolant in oil (head gasket damage from hydrolock attempts). Use only Dex-Cool-compatible coolant (G12++) — mixed coolants accelerate failure.

records.title: Electric Power Steering (Delphi EPS) Column Unit Failure
records.description: Zafira B models fitted with the Delphi/GM electric power steering (EPS) column-mounted unit commonly lose power assistance, often in both directions. The torque/position sensor inside the column-integrated EPS motor unit degrades, and the system stores fault code C1500 (Torque Position Sensor). The fault frequently starts intermittently — assistance cuts out briefly then returns — before becoming permanent, leaving the steering very heavy and hard to turn. This is a recognised failure of the EPS control unit/sensor rather than a hydraulic pump or fluid issue.
records.solution: Diagnose via stored code (C1500). The EPS column unit can be remanufactured/repaired (sensor and electronics rebuilt) by specialists at lower cost than a new genuine unit, or replaced with a new column. Reset/relearn the steering angle sensor after fitment. Check connector and wiring integrity first, as poor connections can mimic the fault.
symptoms: Heavy / hard steering in both directions
Intermittent loss of assist that later becomes permanent

records.title: Front Suspension Control Arm Bolt Corrosion / Breakage (KBA Recall 15411R)
records.description: Later Zafira Tourer/Life models (and related Vivaro vans on the same platform) built between 23 September 2020 and 30 June 2022 were recalled because corrosion of the front suspension control-arm bushing area can cause the control-arm mounting bolt to break. A broken bolt leads to sudden unpredictable handling and potential loss of vehicle control. Around 76,778 vehicles were covered by the German KBA campaign (references 15411R/15414R/15415R).
records.solution: Under the recall, an authorised workshop replaces the screws/bolts and bushings on both sides of the front control arms. Owners should check recall status by VIN and have the work done before further driving if a clunk or handling change is noticed at the front.

records.title: NOx Sensor / SCR System Failure on Euro 6 Diesels (Zafira Tourer C)
records.description: Euro 6 diesel Zafira Tourer C models with SCR/AdBlue (1.6 CDTi B16DTH and 2.0 CDTi B20DTH/D20DTH) commonly suffer NOx sensor failure. The upstream/downstream NOx sensors degrade and report implausible values, setting catalyst-efficiency and NOx-sensor codes (e.g. P20EE, P229F, P118B) and putting the car into reduced power / limp mode with an emissions warning and a restart countdown in some cases. German owners (motor-talk.de) report this as a known fault from around 80,000 km. NOx sensors are relatively expensive genuine parts and often fail again if cheap aftermarket units are used.
records.solution: Diagnose with a scan tool to identify which NOx sensor (position 1 upstream or position 2 downstream) and confirm the SCR catalyst is functioning. Replace the failed NOx sensor with an OE-quality part and clear codes. Verify AdBlue/DEF quality and dosing, and rule out a genuinely degraded SCR catalyst before condemning the sensor.

records.title: Steering Column Intermediate Shaft Loose Press-Fit (Safety Recall R/2010/032)
records.description: Zafira B vehicles built between 16 November 2009 and 24 March 2010 were recalled because the steering column intermediate shaft can have a loose press fit on the upper joint yoke. Over time this develops increasing free play and a knocking noise from the steering column; if ignored, it can ultimately lead to loss of steering control. Approximately 8,854 UK cars were affected under DVSA recall R/2010/032 (launched May 2010). This is a separate, later steering recall to the earlier steering-wheel-controls campaign.
records.solution: Have a new intermediate steering shaft fitted under the manufacturer recall (free of charge). Check the recall status by VIN with an Opel/Vauxhall dealer; any car with knocking or play in the column from this build window should be inspected before further driving.
